title: The charge density fluctuations and the Shrinking Fermi Liquid scenario for strange metallicity in cuprates
authors: Sergio Caprara, Sauri Bhattacharyya, Carlo Di Castro, Giovanni Mirarchi, Götz Seibold, Marco Grilli
abstract: We interpret the strange metal (SM) properties of slightly overdoped cuprates in terms of the recently proposed Shrinking Fermi Liquid theory. This is based on the pervading presence in the cuprate phase diagram of charge density fluctuations (CDF), which have been identified and characterized in RIXS. These fluctuations are abundant and have a low energy due to the proximity of the charge density wave quantum critical point hidden under the superconducting dome of cuprates, but have a short range and non-critical character with a finite energy M/γ~10 meV as measured above Tc. Here M~ ξ^-2 is determined by the short correlation length ξ, while γencodes the Landau damping ruling the lifetime of the charge fluctuations. Besides these low energy CDF, cuprates also display phonons and a broad continuum of particle-hole excitations, mostly due to spin paramagnons arising from their strongly correlated character. With these experimentally characterized ingredients we show that above Tc the SM properties in transport are well described in terms of fermionic Landau quasiparticles scattering with CDF and phonons. The optical properties can instead be interpreted by the combined effect of low energy CDF determining the temperature dependence, and of the paramagnon continuum determining a linear in frequency scattering rate. Remarkably, the combined effect of these simple ingredients also induces ω/T scaling properties for frequencies larger than M/γ. When superconductivity is suppressed by strong magnetic fields the SM properties extend down to a few Kelvin. By assuming that the CDF dissipation parameter γgrows logarithmically by lowering T, we account for all anomalous transport and thermodynamic properties of cuprates (specific heat, Seebeck, heat transport, resistivity, and magnetoresistance) thereby providing a consistent scenario for the SM phase of cuprates.
summary: This paper proposes that the strange metal state in cuprates arises from itinerant fermions scattering off abundant, low-energy Charge Density Fluctuations (CDF). Using the Shrinking Fermi Liquid theory, the authors show this mechanism consistently explains linear-T resistivity and other anomalous transport properties by incorporating CDFs alongside phonons and paramagnons.
main_problem: The paper addresses the anomalous 'Strange Metal' (SM) state observed in slightly overdoped cuprates, characterized by resistivity linear in temperature, which defies standard Fermi Liquid theory.
main_result: The SM behavior is successfully described by interpreting transport properties as scattering between itinerant fermions and low-energy Charge Density Fluctuations (CDF), leading to a consistent model for various anomalous measurements.
method: The authors combine theoretical modeling (Shrinking Fermi Liquid theory) with analysis of experimental data from RIXS and EELS spectroscopy.
model_or_system: The system is the cuprate superconductor, modeled by considering itinerant fermions interacting with low-energy bosonic excitations, specifically Charge Density Fluctuations (CDF), phonons, and spin paramagnons.
key_observables: T-linear resistivity ($ho \propto T$), specific heat coefficient ($\gamma(T)$), Seebeck coefficient ($S/T$), and magnetoresistance.
important_parameters: Low energy scale of CDF ($\omega_{	ext{CDF}} \sim 5-10$ meV) and the finite energy scale $M/\gamma$.
main_assumptions: The core assumption for low-temperature behavior is that the CDF dissipation parameter ($\gamma$) grows logarithmically as temperature decreases when superconductivity is suppressed.
figures_summary: Figure 2 shows RIXS and EELS spectra of Bi2212, decomposing signals to identify elastic peaks, CDFs, phonons, and paramagnon continua.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the SM problem, identifies CDF as the key low-energy scatterer via experimental characterization (RIXS/EELS), develops the Shrinking Fermi Liquid theory framework for transport and optical properties, and finally applies this model to explain multiple anomalous thermodynamic and transport measurements across different doping regimes.
why_interesting: The detailed coupling of fermionic quasiparticles to specific bosonic fluctuations (CDF) provides a concrete mechanism for emergent non-Fermi liquid behavior in strongly correlated materials, which is highly relevant to understanding quantum critical points.
